To undermine something means to weaken it gradually, often in a quiet or hidden way, so that it slowly loses its strength, stability, or effectiveness.

The key word here is gradually. Undermining is not a single, dramatic blow that destroys something instantly. It is a slow, creeping process — like water quietly eroding the foundation of a building over years. The building still looks fine from the outside, but its base is getting weaker and weaker until, eventually, it can no longer stand.

Understanding these three qualities will give you a deep, precise grip on this word.

1. It weakens — it doesn't always destroy (at least not immediately)
Something that is undermined doesn't vanish overnight. It just becomes less strong, less credible, less effective, or less stable than it was before. A leader whose authority is being undermined still holds the title, but people have stopped taking them seriously. The damage is internal.

2. It is gradual
Undermining happens over time, through repeated actions, words, or events. One comment might not undermine your confidence. But a hundred small comments, over months, certainly will.

3. It is often subtle or indirect
This is what makes undermining particularly insidious (sneaky and harmful). It often happens below the surface — through small actions, quiet interference, casual remarks, or behind-the-scenes behavior — rather than through a direct, visible attack. The person being undermined may not even realize what is happening until serious damage has already been done.
Who or What Can Be Undermined?

This verb is extremely versatile. Here are the most common things that get undermined, with examples:

A person's confidence or self-esteem
A manager who constantly criticizes an employee's work in front of others, never acknowledges their successes, and always assigns them tasks they are likely to fail at is undermining that person's confidence. The employee starts doubting their own abilities.

A person's authority or power
Imagine a new school principal who makes decisions. But a senior teacher keeps going around that principal — quietly telling other staff to ignore the new rules, or making decisions without consulting the principal. That teacher is undermining the principal's authority. Over time, the principal can no longer lead effectively because no one respects their power.

Trust in a relationship
If someone repeatedly tells small lies, cancels plans at the last minute, and keeps secrets, they are undermining the trust in that relationship. Trust is being quietly eaten away, even if no single incident is catastrophic.

An argument, theory, or claim
New scientific evidence can undermine an old theory. For example, new data showing that a drug doesn't actually work the way scientists thought it did undermines the original claim about it.

A system, institution, or democracy
Corrupt officials who ignore laws and abuse their power undermine the justice system. When people see that laws are not applied fairly, their faith in the entire system weakens.

Someone's efforts or plans
If you are working hard on a project but a colleague keeps delaying important tasks, withholding information you need, and raising pointless objections in meetings, they are undermining your efforts — making it harder for your work to succeed.

Health
Poor sleep, chronic stress, and a bad diet can undermine your immune system, making your body less able to fight off illness.

This is an important nuance. Undermining can be either deliberate or accidental.

Deliberate: A jealous coworker who wants your job might intentionally undermine you — spreading rumors about you, taking credit for your work, or making you look incompetent in front of your boss. This is a conscious, calculated act.

Unintentional: A well-meaning parent who constantly rescues their child from every difficulty — always doing homework for them, solving every problem, stepping in before the child can struggle — might unknowingly undermine the child's ability to become independent and resilient. There is no bad intention, but the effect is the same: the child's confidence and capability are being weakened.

Notice that undermining almost always works from a position of closeness or from the inside. You undermine things you are near, connected to, or part of. A general undermines their own army from within. A friend undermines your confidence because they are close enough to affect how you feel. An employee undermines company morale from the inside. This is part of why undermining is so effective — and so damaging. It is not an outside threat you can easily see and defend against.

The verb "undermine" typically follows these structures:

  • Someone/Something undermines something: Constant criticism undermines confidence.
  • Someone undermines someone: She felt her colleague was trying to undermine her.
  • Something undermines someone's ability/efforts/position: The scandal undermined the senator's position.

Undermining can happen on a spectrum — from mild to severe.

  • Mild: A single offhand comment that makes you slightly doubt yourself.
  • Moderate: Months of subtle criticism that make you genuinely less confident.
  • Severe: A systematic, long-running campaign that completely destroys someone's credibility, authority, or mental health.

The word works at every point on this spectrum.

• Undermine → the verb (the act itself): She tried to undermine him.
  • Undermining → the present participle / adjective: His undermining behavior was obvious to everyone.
  • Undermined → past tense / adjective: Her confidence was completely undermined.

If you had to boil it down to one sentence:

To undermine something is to slowly and quietly damage its foundation — its strength, its credibility, its effectiveness, or its stability — often from the inside, so that it weakens over time without an obvious, single cause.
